title: Podcast with Julien Camirand Lemyre, Chief Executive Officer & Co-founder at Nord Quantique - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Nord Quantique CEO Julien Camirand Lemyre argues that quantum error-correction redundancy can live inside a single superconducting cavity (GKP and Tesseract bosonic codes) rather than in 100-1,000x more physical qubits, claiming QEC gain has risen from 1.1 in 2024 to above 2 with no post-selection and no classical decoder, with a four-qubit gate-capable system entering operation in 2026 and a 2032 target of 10^-7 to 10^-9 error rates and 2,000+ logical qubits inside 10 square meters. He also frames the company's capital efficiency as deliberate: renting fabs, fridges and benchmarking gear from a Sherbrooke ecosystem built on over a billion dollars of prior public investment.

themes.theme: Redundancy in one cavity, not in 1,000 qubits

insights.claim: Nord Quantique traps multiple microwave photons in a single superconducting resonator to supply the redundancy quantum error correction requires, targeting a one-to-one ratio of cavities to error-corrected qubits instead of the industry's 100-to-1 or 1,000-to-1 physical-qubit overhead.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: If the one-to-one ratio holds, capex and cryogenic footprint per logical qubit collapse relative to transmon roadmaps — the core variable in any quantum hardware valuation.
insights.quote: But nothing tells you that this redundancy that is needed by quantum error correction has to come in the form of more qubits.
insights.locator: So this overhead often comes in the forms of number of qubits

insights.claim: The prevailing physical-to-logical qubit overhead factor for quantum error correction sits somewhere between 100 and 1,000, which is what forces the industry toward ever-larger systems.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The 100-1,000x overhead is the denominator that determines how much hardware any fault-tolerant roadmap must actually ship and finance.
insights.quote: And usually this factor is somewhere between 100 to 1,000.
insights.locator: So this overhead often comes in the forms of number of qubits

insights.claim: Nord Quantique's grid-state (GKP) qubits differ from Alice & Bob's cat qubits in that a single qubit corrects both X and Z errors rather than suppressing only one error channel, per the company's early-2024 demonstration paper.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Distinguishes two bosonic bets: biased-noise cat qubits still need an outer code, while grid states claim full correction in one mode — a fork worth tracking when comparing bosonic startups.
insights.quote: In these qubits, you can do full quantum error correction on a single of these qubits, so correcting for both X and Z errors
insights.locator: Yeah, definitely. So bosonic codes is a large space

insights.claim: Storing photons of different frequencies in the same cavity yields multimode codes such as the Tesseract code, released in 2025, meaning code upgrades can be deployed on existing hardware without rebuilding the architecture.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Software-like upgradeability of the error-correction layer shortens the improvement cycle versus competitors who must re-fab chips for each new code.
insights.quote: As long as we have enough modes in our cavity, this is something that we can do on the fly as well.
insights.locator: I think it, like, first of all, it’s impressive

insights.claim: Error correction on Nord Quantique's cavities runs autonomously without the classical syndrome-measurement decoding layer that conventional QEC architectures require.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Removing the real-time classical decoder removes a latency and control-electronics cost center that scales badly for surface-code machines.
insights.quote: So all the error correction that we’re running here is done autonomously, which is another differentiator of the quantum operation on that system.
insights.locator: Yeah, yeah, so we’re looking at, so depending

themes.theme: Measured QEC gain and where fidelity actually sits

insights.claim: Nord Quantique's internally tracked quantum error correction gain has moved from roughly 1.1 at the time of its 2024 memory demonstration to above 2 today, i.e. error correction now more than doubles hardware performance rather than barely breaking even.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: QEC gain is the single cleanest metric for whether a bosonic platform is past break-even; a 1.1 to 2+ move in about two years sets the slope to extrapolate.
insights.quote: So I think we had a factor of 1.1 at that time. Now we’re beyond two
insights.locator: 100% error correction, yeah. So no post-selection

insights.claim: The 2024 Nord Quantique result was a quantum memory demonstration with full error correction and no post-selection; gate operations came later and have been shown at conferences and on the company's blog rather than in that paper.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Memory-only demos are routinely marketed as computing milestones; the gate/memory distinction is the due-diligence question for any bosonic claim.
insights.quote: Yeah, so this paper in 2024 was a demonstration as a quantum memory.
insights.locator: If we just go into the 2024 paper

insights.claim: Current single-cavity operation fidelity at Nord Quantique is around three nines (99.9%), with two-qubit performance still improving — far short of the six-to-nine nines needed for useful fault tolerance.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Anchors the gap between today's hardware and utility: three nines now versus a 10^-7 to 10^-9 target means six orders of magnitude to close by 2032.
insights.quote: so I think we’re talking around three nines is what we are working with right now in terms of operation on a single cavity
insights.locator: Could you explain what that means?

insights.claim: In the Tesseract code experiment, turning on post-selection shut off an error channel entirely and drove logical decay below the experiment's measurement floor, while the non-post-selected mode matched GKP performance.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: An unmeasurably low logical decay rate is the strongest evidence offered for the multimode scaling path — but it is a post-selected number, so treat it as an upper bound on promise, not deliverable performance.
insights.quote: we were not able to measure it at that point, meaning that the decay was extremely low for that experiment
insights.locator: Yeah, so I think it’s, so what we have to do is more of the same

themes.theme: 2032 roadmap: error rate, logical count, footprint

insights.claim: Nord Quantique targets 10^-7 to 10^-9 error rates in a single cavity by around 2032, achieved through successive multimode code improvements rather than a new hardware architecture.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated milestone to score the company against; slippage past 2032 or a switch away from the single-cavity claim would invalidate the whole capital-efficiency thesis.
insights.quote: So we think we can reach 10 to the minus seven to 10 to the minus nine error rates, which in single cavity with these multiple techniques.
insights.locator: Yeah, so I think it’s, so what we have to do is more of the same

insights.claim: The company's system design aims to fit more than 2,000 logical qubits inside a 10 square meter cryogenic footprint, sidestepping the multi-fridge scaling layer that conventional superconducting machines require.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Footprint per logical qubit is an underrated cost driver — datacenter floor, dilution refrigerators and wiring — and 2,000 logical qubits in 10 m2 would be a step change in siting economics.
insights.quote: So something that will fit into 10 meters squared for more than 2000 of these logical qubits.
insights.locator: Yeah, thank you. Yeah, so we’re based on a superconducting platform

insights.claim: A four-qubit, gate-capable Nord Quantique system goes into operation this year and will be the company's first more public release, run with partners directly on error-corrected qubits.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The near-term checkpoint: if the four-qubit machine slips or ships without gates, the 2032 roadmap loses its first datapoint.
insights.quote: So this will be in operation this year and also something that we intend to work with partner to be operating with all these gates
insights.locator: What can we see in this? So we already have demonstrated gates

insights.claim: The six-year gap to the 2032 targets is attributed mainly to engineering, integration and scaling work plus purpose-built simulation and QEC tooling for bosonic hardware — not to unsolved algorithmic problems or a funding shortfall.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Framing the remaining risk as execution rather than physics is the bull case; it also means the milestone is schedule-risk sensitive and headcount-driven.
insights.quote: I think a lot of the simulation tools we had to build, how we do quantum error correction for this hardware is also specific to that hardware.
insights.locator: More money is always welcome, of course

themes.theme: Capital efficiency rented from a public ecosystem

insights.claim: Nord Quantique's capital efficiency is a deliberate structural choice: as a spin-off of Sherbrooke's Institut Quantique it rents superconducting fabs, dilution fridges and benchmarking facilities rather than building them, leveraging over a billion dollars of prior Quebec and Canadian infrastructure investment.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Public-infrastructure leverage is a real, quantifiable moat for regional hardware startups — and a template for comparing burn rates across quantum hardware companies.
insights.quote: But we didn’t have to pay for this. Like, this was there, we’re just renting the access.
insights.locator: No, no, no. It’s by design

insights.claim: The Sherbrooke and Bromont cluster sits in what Lemyre calls the Northeastern Semiconductor Manufacturing Corridor running down to Albany, hosting IBM packaging and Teledyne plants and a tech-transfer culture that supplies both microelectronics talent and fabrication access.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Maps quantum hardware capability onto existing semiconductor geography — the same corridor logic that drives packaging and advanced-node investment decisions.
insights.quote: it is part of what we call the Northeastern Semiconductor Manufacturing Corridor that runs all the way down to Albany, ends up here in Sherbrooke and in Bromont
insights.locator: No, no, no. It’s by design

insights.claim: The rent-the-infrastructure model has a defined end date as Nord Quantique scales, but reduced QEC overhead means the systems it must eventually build in-house are physically smaller and therefore cheaper.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: The capex step-up is coming; the question for investors is whether overhead reduction offsets the loss of subsidized infrastructure.
insights.locator: So that model where we rent a lot of the infrastructure has an end

insights.claim: Nord Quantique is in discussions for its first system sale, and explicitly does not plan to sell systems in volume — the strategy is a small number of placements with application partners until commercially viable, error-corrected machines exist.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Revenue will stay lumpy and thin near-term; anyone modeling this business on unit volume is modeling the wrong company.
insights.quote: I think selling a ton of systems is not something that we will see from Nord.
insights.locator: Yeah. So right now we are in discussions for a sale of a system

insights.claim: Lemyre concedes the four-qubit machine will run no useful algorithms; its purpose is to let partners benchmark how algorithms behave when an error-correction layer is running underneath them.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Unusually candid for a hardware vendor — useful as a calibration point against peers marketing small systems as application-ready.
insights.quote: So we won’t run any useful algorithms on those.
insights.locator: I think, yeah, you’re right. So we won’t run any useful algorithms

themes.theme: Modality view: speed, transmon walls, high-rate codes

insights.claim: Recent high-rate code results from Harvard and others that slash physical-qubit requirements are read as validating rather than threatening the bosonic bet, because Nord Quantique believes its qubit-count-versus-clock-rate trade-off is favorable and new codes can be loaded onto existing cavities.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Watch the clock-rate axis: platforms that cut qubit counts by paying in cycle time may lose on time-to-solution even with fewer qubits.
insights.quote: It’s also the trade-off between number of qubits and clock rate, we believe is good with the bosonic codes that we have right now.
insights.locator: I think it, like, first of all, it’s impressive

insights.claim: Standard transmon-based superconducting architectures face a specific scaling wall in networking multiple dilution refrigerators together, a problem the community has not yet solved.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Multi-fridge interconnect is the concrete technical bottleneck to probe when assessing IBM-style superconducting roadmaps; it is also the constraint Nord Quantique's small-footprint claim is designed to avoid.
insights.quote: I do think this more standard transmon-based approach faces some challenges, especially when it comes to like connecting multiple fridges into a network environment.
insights.locator: That’s a good question. It’s a tricky one

insights.claim: Speed is the durable advantage Nord Quantique claims to inherit from the superconducting platform, retaining fast operation rates for bosonic qubits even as it abandons the transmon design.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Clock speed is the axis where superconducting platforms beat neutral atoms and trapped ions; it survives the switch to bosonic encoding.
insights.quote: So the technology is fast. We keep that operation rate functioning for our bosonic qubits.
insights.locator: That’s a good question. It’s a tricky one

insights.claim: The pace of progress in the quantum error correction field across superconducting and neutral-atom platforms is what has most surprised Nord Quantique's CEO over the past couple of years, and he expects systems to move from demonstrating QEC to integrating and scaling it.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Signals the sector's next narrative shift: from one-off QEC demos to QEC as a shipped, integrated subsystem — the point at which hardware differentiation becomes measurable.
insights.quote: I would say that the rate of evolution of the quantum error correction field
insights.locator: And as you think about the market evolution

insights.claim: Michel Devoret, credited in the interview as a 2026 Nobel Prize winner and the founder of bosonic-code demonstrations in superconducting circuits, is actively visiting and tied to the Sherbrooke ecosystem Nord Quantique spun out of.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Nobel-level validation of the bosonic approach plus local proximity is soft evidence for talent gravity around the Quebec cluster.
insights.quote: he’s the founder of this demonstration of bosonic codes in superconducting circuits
insights.locator: It’s funny because I was just at dinner with Michel Devoret
